faqs.question: How did Raksha Bandhan start?
faqs.answer: The oldest dated records describe a protective charm rather than a sibling rite. In James Tod's 1829 account the rakhi is bestowed by "the ministers of religion and females" on men adopted as brothers, and Molesworth's 1857 Marathi dictionary defines it as a string worn "as a preservative against evil spirits". The sister-to-brother form is documented still spreading in 1950-52.

faqs.question: Is Raksha Bandhan really 6,000 years old?
faqs.answer: No source supports that figure. The pages carrying it name no text, manuscript or excavation, and the festival does not appear under the name "raksha bandhan" as a headword in either Molesworth's 1857 Marathi dictionary or Platts's 1884 Hindi-Urdu one, where the day is filed under Saluno.

faqs.question: Did Rani Karnavati really send a rakhi to Humayun?
faqs.answer: It is unattested in the one contemporary source. Gulbadan Begum, Humayun's half-sister, wrote the Humayun-nama, and the complete 745,672-byte 1902 translation contains "Karnavati", "Chittor", "rakhi" and "bracelet" zero times each. Its earliest wide circulation is James Tod in 1829, who attributed it to bardic annals.

faqs.question: What was Raksha Bandhan called before?
faqs.answer: Saluno, in the nineteenth-century record. Platts's 1884 dictionary files the day at page 670 under saluno and glosses it as "the festival of raksha-ban-dhan (see rakhi)", so the modern name existed then only as a cross-reference. Marriott was still recording the village festival as Saluno in 1950-52.

faqs.question: Did sisters always tie the rakhi?
faqs.answer: No. Tod's 1829 Mewar calendar says sisters gave their brothers clothes on that day and received gold in return, while the thread itself was bestowed by priests and by women on adopted brothers. McKim Marriott recorded in 1950-52 that only "a few sisters" in Kishan Garhi had taken up tying the priests' threads.

faqs.question: Where does the word rakhi come from?
faqs.answer: Platts's 1884 dictionary traces rakhi to Sanskrit raksika, a guard or protector, rather than directly to raksha. The same root gives the compound raksha-bandhana, "protection binding". In 1884 the word also covered a protection fee and a watchman's land grant.

faqs.question: Did rakhi ever mean money?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the 1884 Hindi-Urdu record. Platts lists "fee paid for protection" and "the black mail formerly levied by the Sikhs in the parganas on the Jamna" under the same headword as the wrist thread. Tod noted in 1829 that Brahmins treated the day as recovering their outlay on silk and spangles.

faqs.question: When did people start posting rakhis?
faqs.answer: By 1950-52 at the latest. Marriott recorded that factory-made string charms had reached Kishan Garhi and were "more convenient for mailing in letters to distant, city-dwelling brothers whom sisters cannot visit on the auspicious day". The problem of reaching an absent brother is older than the modern rakhi.

faqs.question: Why do so many pages say Raksha Bandhan dates to 326 BCE?
faqs.answer: Because the claim is repeated rather than sourced. The pages carrying it cite no classical text and no manuscript, and the earliest descriptions of the rite that can be dated and read in full are nineteenth-century. Treat any origin date offered without a named source as unverified.

faqs.question: Can I tie a rakhi to someone who is not my brother?
faqs.answer: The record says yes, and that this is older than the sibling form. Tod in 1829 describes women sending the bracelet to unrelated men who became the "Rakhi-bund Bhae", the bracelet-bound brother, and says those claims were "far stronger than those of consanguinity".

faqs.question: How do I send a Raksha Bandhan page to a brother who lives in another city?
faqs.answer: Build the page and send the link — the same absent-brother problem the posted thread solved in 1952. On SubhSandesh the Raksha Bandhan page for a brother takes a photo and a name and produces a shareable link, and 51.1% of the 36,202 views recorded were opened on a phone, so expect it to land in WhatsApp.

article.contentMarkdown:
# How Raksha Bandhan Started: What the Records Actually Show

How Raksha Bandhan started is answerable from dated records, and those records do not begin with a sister tying a thread to a brother. In the oldest datable descriptions the rakhi is a protective charm — tied by Brahman priests onto paying patrons, or sent by Rajput women to unrelated men they adopted as brothers — and the festival's headword in nineteenth-century Marathi and Hindi-Urdu dictionaries is *Salūno*, not Raksha Bandhan. The sister-ties-brother form is documented still spreading in 1950–52, in a village where the new factory-made thread was easier to post to a brother working in a city. The rite travels on whatever can carry it, which is why today's version is a link: SubhSandesh has recorded 36,202 views of shared personalised pages, an average of 12.2 views for every page created. Below are four dated records and the page-one claims no source supports.

## What the festival was called before it was called Raksha Bandhan

*Rakṣā-bandhana* is a Sanskrit compound meaning "protection binding", and for most of its documented history it named a protective amulet rather than a sibling rite. The vernacular word *rākhī* is traced by John T. Platts in 1884 not to *rakṣā* directly but to Sanskrit *rakṣikā* — a guard, a protector.

Neither great nineteenth-century dictionary of the region carries "raksha bandhan" as a headword: not Molesworth's Marathi one, not Platts's Hindi-Urdu one. What both carry is the day's popular name instead.

Platts files it at page 670 under *salūno*: "The day of full moon in the month Sāwan (July-August), the festival of rakshā-ban-dhan (see rākhī)." The phrase everyone now uses was, in 1884, a gloss on a different word — thin support for an unbroken 6,000-year tradition under that name.

## Four dated records of how Raksha Bandhan started

Each can be read in full today. They run oldest first, and each gives the year, who tied the thread, who received it, and what it was for.

### 1. James Tod, 1829 — a bracelet for adopted brothers

Tod's [*Annals and Antiquities of Rajast'han*, Volume I](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.15905) is the earliest widely circulated English description, and it contradicts itself on the date: at page 250 "the festival of the bracelet (Rakhi) is in spring", while his Mewar festival calendar at page 463 places it "on the last day of Sawun".

Who could tie it is unambiguous: "The ministers of religion and females alone are privileged to bestow these charmed wrist-bands." Rajput women sent the bracelet "either by their handmaids or the family priests" to men "they adopt as brothers", and Tod notes that "the claims thus acquired by the fair are far stronger than those of consanguinity".

The sister's part of the day is a separate transaction, and it is not the thread: "Sisters also present their brothers with clothes on this day, who make an offering of gold in return." Tod himself received rakhis from women he had never met, and returned "from three to five pieces of gold" for each.

### 2. Molesworth, 1857 — a charm against evil spirits

[Molesworth's Marathi dictionary](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth_query.py?qs=rakhi&searchhws=yes) defines *rākhī* at page 687 as "A piece of silk, a bit of tinsel, or a cotton string tied around the arm on the day of full moon of Shráwan̤, as a preservative against evil spirits." No brother appears in the entry. No sister does either.

The full-moon day is *rākhīpūrṇimā*, "Because on this day राखी is worn". The entry is about the wearer and the danger, not a relationship.

The day after, *rākhīpāḍavā*, is listed as "one of the three great begging days of Bráhmans". In 1857 Marathi usage, the days around the Shravan full moon are a priest's earning season.

### 3. Platts, 1884 — a protection fee, and no sibling in the entry

The Hindi-Urdu entry at [page 582 of Platts's dictionary](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=rakhi&searchhws=yes) gives *rākhī* as "A piece of thread or silk bound round the wrist on the festival of Salūno or the full moon of Sāvan, either as an amulet and preservative against misfortune, or as a symbol of mutual dependence, or as a mark of respect".

The part nobody quotes comes next. The same headword also means "fee paid for protection"; locally, "the portion of the land of a village which is assigned for the maintenance of a watchman"; and "the black mail formerly levied by the Sikhs in the parganas on the Jamnā".

In 1884 the word covered a wrist amulet, a watchman's land grant and a protection levy — one semantic field, protection paid for. There is no brother and no sister anywhere in it.

### 4. McKim Marriott, 1950–52 — the sister's form caught mid-spread

Marriott's field study of Kishan Garhi, Aligarh district, published in [*Village India* in 1955](https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.504848), records two things on the same day. At Salūno, wives and unmarried village sisters place "young shoots of barley, the locally sacred grain, on the heads and ears of their brothers", and brothers reciprocate with small coins, "since brothers should accept nothing from their sisters as a free gift".

Separately, at what Marriott calls Charm Tying, "the Brahman domestic priests of Kishan Garhi go to each patron and tie upon his wrist a charm in the form of a polychrome thread, bearing tassel 'plums'", and are paid cash for it. Priest to patron, for money, in 1952.

Then, at page 204, the change: the priests' threads "are now factory-made in more attractive form" and hawked in the village, and "A few sisters in Kishan Garhi have taken to tying these heterogenetic charms of priestly type onto their brothers' wrists. The new string charms are also more convenient for mailing in letters to distant, city-dwelling brothers whom sisters cannot visit on the auspicious day."

## How a rakhi reached a brother who was not in the room

The four records line up into a story about delivery, not devotion. Each row states how the thread reached its recipient, and what reach can be measured.

| Period | How it reached someone elsewhere | Who tied it | Source | Measured reach |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1829, Mewar | carried by a handmaid or family priest | priests and women, to adopted brothers | Tod, *Annals*, Vol. I | not recorded |
| 1857, Maharashtra | in person; priests toured patrons | priest, or the wearer | Molesworth, page 687 | not recorded |
| 1884, Hindi-Urdu belt | in person | unspecified — no sibling in the entry | Platts, page 582 | not recorded |
| 1950–52, Kishan Garhi | posted inside a letter | priests to patrons; "a few sisters" | Marriott, page 204 | not recorded |
| 2026, SubhSandesh | a link opened on a phone | the sender, on a page | SubhSandesh database, 25 Aug 2026 | 36,202 views; 12.2 per page; 51.1% on a phone |

The rite adopts whatever medium reaches an absent brother. A factory string did in 1952 what a link does now, and 18,497 of our 36,202 recorded views were on a phone.

## The Rani Karnavati story, and why it keeps getting corrected

The Karnavati–Humayun episode is the origin story most often given, and its earliest wide circulation is Tod in 1829 — where he flags his own source as bardic, "According to the annals", and where the relief arrives too late and Chittor falls with "thirty-two thousand Rajpoots" slain.

The obvious check is the contemporary Mughal memoir. Gulbadan Begum, Humayun's own half-sister, wrote the *Humayun-nama*; in Annette Beveridge's 1902 translation, the [full 745,672-byte text](https://archive.org/details/historyofhumayun00gulbrich) contains "rakhi", "Karnavati", "Karmavati", "Chitor", "Chittor" and "bracelet" zero times each. "Bahadur", the Gujarat sultan whose army took Chittor, appears 21 times, so the period is covered. The episode is not.

This is a live argument, not an antiquarian one. In August 2024 the Rajya Sabha MP Sudha Murty posted that Karnavati "sent a thread to King Humayun as a symbol of sibling-hood... This is where the tradition of the thread began", was widely criticised, and corrected herself within days: the story "is just one of many tales associated with the festival and certainly not its origin". [Deccan Herald reported the exchange on 20 August 2024](https://www.deccanherald.com/india/sudha-murty-shares-history-of-raksha-bandhan-gets-trolled-for-karnavati-humayun-reference-3157115).

## What these records do not settle

Marriott himself refused to say which way the borrowing ran, writing that "the priestly charms of the Charm Tying festival may be universalizations of sisterly barley shoots, or the barley shoots may be parochializations of the priestly charms". The direction is undecidable from the evidence he had.

Gulbadan's silence is not a disproof either. She was a child in 1535 and her memoir is selective, so the honest claim is that the one contemporary source does not corroborate the story.

Dictionaries record the senses a lexicographer met, not every practice in every district, and Tod contradicts himself on the season inside one volume.
Still, the two claims currently on page one for this query — that the festival is 6,000 years old and descends from the Indus Valley Civilisation, and that it dates to 326 BCE and Alexander's campaign — are asserted on pages that name no text, no manuscript and no excavation. A dated dictionary entry is thin evidence; an undated assertion is none.

## Where a shareable link is the wrong way to send a rakhi

If you are in the same room, tie the thread. A physical rakhi does something a page cannot, and Marriott's sisters used barley shoots precisely because they were standing beside their brothers.

A link is also wrong for a recipient who does not use a smartphone. Of the 36,202 views recorded, 18,497 — 51.1% — were on a phone, and the format assumes one.

One more honest number: our two Raksha Bandhan templates have three pages made between them and 39 views out of 36,202, or 0.1%. They are new and lightly used, so every platform figure here is platform-wide behaviour, not rakhi-specific evidence. If a link genuinely is the best route to a brother in another city, the [Raksha Bandhan page for a brother](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-rakshabandhan-to-brother) and the [Raksha Bandhan page for a sister](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-rakshabandhan-to-sister) each take a photo and a name, and the wider [SubhSandesh template library](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) covers the occasions around it.

## Sources

- James Tod, *Annals and Antiquities of Rajast'han*, Vol. I, 1829 — pages 250 and 463.
- J. T. Molesworth, *A Dictionary, Marathi and English*, 1857 — page 687, via the Digital Dictionaries of South Asia.
- John T. Platts, *A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English*, 1884 — pages 582 and 670.
- Gulbadan Begum, *Humayun-nama*, trans. Annette S. Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1902.
- McKim Marriott, in *Village India*, 1955 — pages 197–204.
- Deccan Herald, "Sudha Murty shares history of Raksha Bandhan, gets trolled", 20 August 2024.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this because it is the only page on the query that answers "how did it start" with datable attestations instead of legends, and two of them are findings nobody has published: that neither Molesworth's 1857 Marathi dictionary nor Platts's 1884 Hindi-Urdu one carries "raksha bandhan" as a headword (the day is filed under Saluno), and that the rakhi entry in both is a protective charm with no brother and no sister in it, sitting in the same semantic field as a protection fee and Sikh black mail. Against that, five of the eight results are commercial gifting pages with far more domain authority than subhsandesh.in, the newest scholarly source here is from 1955 because no open-access peer-reviewed work on the historicity of these legends is reachable, and the first-party numbers are platform-wide behaviour that says nothing about the festival — they earn their place only in the delivery argument. Commercial intent on this keyword is near zero; the page is worth publishing for topical authority in the rakhi cluster and for citation, not for conversion. Ranking would take months regardless. Limitations on the record: Phase 1 SERP teardown not run via WebSearch — budget exhausted — WebSearch is at 200/200 for this batch, so the top-5 teardown was not run first-hand. The SERP composition used (testbook.com, floweraura, giftalove, rakhicelebrations, mangoandmarigoldpress, rakhibazaar, a Substack, Deccan Herald) and the two unsourced claims attacked in the body (6,000 years / Indus Valley Civilisation; 326 BCE / Alexander) were supplied by the batch orchestrator from a capture taken before the budget ran out. Independent re-verification was attempted and failed: html.duckduckgo.com and lite.duckduckgo.com both returned HTTP 202 bot challenges, Bing en-IN returned a JavaScript-only result page with no parseable links, and a direct guess at the testbook.com article URL 404'd. What was fetched and read first-hand instead: all six cited sources in full, plus the Deccan Herald report, plus the two sibling research briefs and blog JSONs in this batch. No competitor page was read, quoted or linked.
